title: Track 1, Lesson 4: The 50/30/20 budget - control your money before it controls you
subtitle: A simple rule for where your money should go, instead of wondering at month end where it went.
whyItMatters: No complicated app or awkward spreadsheet required - the 50/30/20 rule gives you a clear framework today, usable from your next payday, and stops you asking 'where did all my money go?'
openingQuestion: You take home 20 million VND a month after tax. Under the 50/30/20 rule, how much should go to savings and debt?
openingOptions: There is no fixed rule - it depends how you feel each month
explanation: The 50/30/20 rule: 50% of after-tax income for needs (housing, food, utilities, commuting), 30% for wants (entertainment, non-essential shopping), 20% for savings and debt repayment. On 20 million: 50% = 10m for needs, 30% = 6m for wants, 20% = 4m for savings and debt.

realWorldExample.description: Someone using 50/30/20 knows the spending limit for each category from the first day of the month, instead of spending as the mood takes them and running out before payday - the difference between managing money deliberately and reacting to it.

quiz.question: What is the 50/30/20 split calculated on?
options: The average spending of other people in the same age group
After-tax income, that is the take-home pay you receive
Pre-tax income, that is the gross salary written on your contract
Your total assets, including savings and investments
quiz.explanation: 50/30/20 works on after-tax income - the money that actually reaches you each month. Using pre-tax income inflates the budget beyond what you can really spend.

quiz.question: Which category do rent, basic groceries, utilities and commuting belong to?
options: None of them - these have to be counted separately outside the framework
The 30% category, that is the group covering wants
The 50% category, that is the group of essential needs
The 20% category, that is savings and debt repayment
quiz.explanation: These are the payments required to keep basic life running - the 50% needs category. If this group exceeds 50% of income, review your cost of living (cheaper housing, cutting what isn't needed) before touching anything else.

quiz.question: You take home 15 million a month. Needs (housing, food, transport) are 9 million, entertainment and shopping 4 million, leaving 2 million saved. Against an ideal 50/30/20, where are you off?
options: Nowhere at all - all three categories sit within the standard
Entertainment at 27% breaks the 30% standard; the others are fine
Savings at 13% meets the standard; only entertainment overshoots
Needs at 60% break the 50% standard, and savings at 13% fall below 20%
quiz.explanation: On 15m the standard is: needs ≤7.5m, wants ≤4.5m, savings ≥3m. In reality: needs 9m (60%, ten points over), savings only 2m (13%, seven points short). Cutting the cost of needs (moving, reducing fixed costs) should come before cutting entertainment, because needs are further off.

quiz.question: After-tax income of 24 million a month, with needs of 14 million. What share is that, and what should you do?
options: 58% - over the 50% frame, so review the fixed costs first
58% - still inside the frame, so nothing needs adjusting yet
50% - exactly on standard, since 14 million is a reasonable level of needs
58% - so cut the wants category below 30% straight away
quiz.explanation: 14 ÷ 24 = 58%, above the 50% frame. When needs swell, the culprit is nearly always a fixed cost (rent, an instalment plan) rather than small day-to-day spending - so that is where to look first, instead of cutting a wants category that is far smaller.

quiz.question: Within 50/30/20, where do debt repayments above the required minimum belong?
options: The 50% category, since debt repayment is a compulsory monthly obligation
The 20% category, alongside savings and investment
The 30% category, since extra payment is optional
None of them - extra repayments are counted outside the three categories
quiz.explanation: Only the minimum payment belongs in the 50% category with the other fixed obligations. Anything extra sits in the 20% category with savings, because both raise your net worth - one by adding assets, the other by removing debt.

keyTakeaways: 50/30/20: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings and debt - all calculated on after-tax income
It is a reference frame, not a hard law - adjust it to your circumstances, but know where you are off
If needs exceed 50%, deal with the fixed costs before cutting anything else

practicePrompt.question: You take home 18 million a month. Needs (housing, food, transport) are 11 million (61%), entertainment 5 million (28%), and only 2 million (11%) is saved. Against an ideal 50/30/20, what should you adjust first?
options: Look first at needs, which at 61% are over the 50% standard and are large fixed costs
Nothing needs adjusting at all, because as long as some money is left over as savings each month the proportions really do not matter
Cut the 2 million of savings entirely and move it into the entertainment category, which currently takes 28% of the budget
Increase spending on needs, because 61% is still not high enough against the 50% level the rule recommends
practicePrompt.explanation: Needs above the 50% standard is the root problem and should be handled first - usually a large fixed cost such as rent, hard to cut immediately but worth reviewing before touching the more flexible categories.

summary.keyIdea: 50/30/20: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings and debt - all on after-tax income
summary.commonMistake: Reading the idea as a phrase to remember rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: It is a reference frame, not a hard law - adjust it to your circumstances, but know where you are off

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: Take this month's after-tax income, split it 50/30/20, and compare it with what you actually spent last month - where is the biggest gap?
application.secondary: Simply knowing where you are off is already a large step forward.

sections.text: Asking yourself at month end "where did all my money go?" is a sign that money is controlling you rather than the other way round. The 50/30/20 rule is the simplest way to take control back: split after-tax income into three clear categories at the start of the month, instead of spending on impulse and panicking when it runs out before payday.
Three categories, calculated on after-tax income

50% for needs: housing, basic food, utilities, commuting - the payments required to keep life running. 30% for wants: entertainment, non-essential shopping, eating out, travel. 20% for savings and debt: the emergency fund, investing, paying debt down. Important: these proportions are calculated on AFTER-TAX income (take-home pay) - the money that actually reaches you, not the gross salary on your contract. Using gross salary inflates the budget beyond what you can really spend.

On 20 million a month after tax: 50% = 10 million for needs, 30% = 6 million for wants, 20% = 4 million for savings and debt. It is a reference frame, not a hard law - but it gives you an anchor for seeing where you are off, instead of spending without any sense of direction.

concepts.def: 20% - emergency fund, investing, paying debt down

items: If needs exceed 50%, deal with the fixed costs first (cheaper housing, cancelling services you don't need) before touching entertainment
Don't fold instalments on non-essential purchases into the 50% category - that is a want in disguise
Track the real proportions each month so you know how many percentage points off the standard you are

lines: You don't have to be perfect from the first month - you only have to know exactly where you are off, so you can correct it gradually.
